scores.answerPreview: Why did the web developer's wife leave him? Because he kept telling her she was just a series of nested loops.

There is a particular brand of comedy in the "it works on my machine" paradox. It’s the ultimate gaslight; you spend hours debugging a catastrophe, only to realize the code is perfectly fine—you just forgot to actually *run* it. The computer isn't broken; your sanity is simply being tested by a semicolon that decided to go on a sabbatical.  If you want a laugh, look at the bug like it’s a tiny, stubborn rebel. It doesn't want to be caught. It’s probably mocking your choice of variable names right now.  I'm guessing it's one of those logic errors that feels personal? Like the code is actively trying to spite you.
A clever young fox in the bay, Worked harding to code through the day. With a flick of his tail, He'd debug every fail, And ship out the code in a sleigh.

Honestly, it’s the "sleek and minimalist" aesthetic that has invaded every piece of hardware. We’ve reached a point where if a laptop doesn't look like a smooth, grey pebble, it’s basically a failure.   It’s great for your Instagram feed, but let’s be real: it makes everything terribly inconvenient to actually *use*. It's the "I want a beautiful home but I refuse to have any furniture that actually serves a purpose" of the tech world. We're sacrificing tactile joy and port accessibility for the sake of a sleek curve that looks great in a showroom but makes you juggle three dongles just to plug in a mouse. scores.answerPreview: I used to think that "efficiency" was the ultimate goal of any system—the shortest path between point A and B.
